title: Emergency Placement
statement: Placing a child with a relative or close family friend right away, before the full approval process is finished.
source_says: shall initiate an assessment ... no later than five business days after the placement
steps: Opened public.law WIC 309, read subd. (d)(1)-(2): relative or nonrelative extended family member may ask for emergency placement; after the 361.4 assessment the child may be placed on an emergency basis, then the home goes through resource family approval under 16519.5, starting within five business days.

title: Emergency Placement
statement: The county first does a walk-through of the home and background and child abuse record checks on the adults who live there.
source_says: Conduct an in-home inspection to assess the safety of the home ... All persons over 18 years of age living in the home
steps: Opened public.law WIC 361.4, read (a)(1) in-home inspection, (a)(2)(A) criminal records check of all persons over 18 living in the home, (a)(3) prior abuse or neglect check of the caregiver and other adults in the home.

title: Emergency Placement
statement: When a child goes to stay with family right away, after quick safety checks.
source_says: Conduct an in-home inspection to assess the safety of the home
steps: Same two pages as the definition. 'Family' here also covers a nonrelative extended family member under 309(d); the simple line does not change the meaning.

title: Fit and Willing Relative
statement: One of the permanent plans a judge can choose: the child stays long term with a relative who is able and willing to care for them, without adoption or guardianship.
source_says: Order that the child be permanently placed with a fit and willing relative
steps: Opened public.law WIC 366.26, read the subd. (b) list: it is item 6, separate from adoption (1), tribal customary adoption (2) and guardianship (3),(5). Also opened the Self-Help parents guide, which lists 'Placed permanently with a fit and willing relative' as its own option.

title: Fit and Willing Relative
statement: A long-term home with a relative who is able and willing.
source_says: Placed permanently with a fit and willing relative
steps: Opened selfhelp.courts.ca.gov guide-parents, read the list of long-term plan preferences.

title: Foster Parent
statement: An adult who is approved to give a temporary home to a child who cannot live with their parents right now.
source_says: eligible to provide foster care for children in out-of-home placement
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16519.5, read (c)(1) resource family definition ('an individual or family that has successfully met both' standards) and (c)(4)(A).

title: Foster Parent
statement: Foster parents get training and support and take care of the child day to day while the case goes on.
source_says: completes a minimum of 12 hours of preapproval caregiver training ... complete a minimum of eight hours of caregiver training annually
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16519.5, read the training rule in (g) and 'A county may provide supportive services' in (p)(5).

title: Foster Parent
statement: California now calls approved foster homes resource families.
source_says: to replace the existing multiple processes for licensing foster family homes ... This approval is in lieu of a foster family home license
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16519.5, read (a) and (c)(5).

title: Foster Parent
statement: An adult who is approved to take care of a child for a while.
source_says: eligible to provide foster care for children in out-of-home placement
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: Foster Youth Bill of Rights
statement: A California law that lists all the rights that children and youth in foster care have
source_says: broad expressions of the rights of children in foster care and are not exhaustive of all rights set forth in the United States Constitution and the California Constitution
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16001.9. Subd. (a) lists rights for 'All children placed in foster care', but (b) says the list is not exhaustive, so 'all the rights' goes too far.
fix: A California law that lists many of the rights that children and youth in foster care have. Youth have other rights too.

title: Foster Youth Bill of Rights
statement: including the right to be safe, to go to school, to see siblings, to have privacy, to participate in activities, and much more
source_says: To live in a safe, healthy, and comfortable home ... To attend school ... To visit and contact siblings, family members, and relatives privately, unless prohibited by court order
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16001.9, read subd. (a) items on safe home, school, siblings, privacy, and 'To participate in extracurricular, cultural, racial, ethnic, personal enrichment, and social activities'. Sibling visits are 'unless prohibited by court order'.

title: Foster Youth Bill of Rights
statement: The list of rights every kid in foster care has.
source_says: All children placed in foster care, either voluntarily
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16001.9, read the opening of subd. (a). The page also says 'These rights also apply to nonminor dependents in foster care.'

title: Foster Youth Education Liaison
statement: Every school district has a staff person whose job is to help students in foster care.
source_says: Each local educational agency shall designate a staff person as the educational liaison for foster children.
steps: Opened public.law Ed Code 48853.5, read subd. (c). The statute says 'local educational agency', which is wider than school district; the page did not define the term.

title: Foster Youth Education Liaison
statement: The liaison helps a child enroll right away, stay in the same school after a move, and get school records and credits transferred.
source_says: Ensure and facilitate the proper educational placement, enrollment in school, and checkout ... proper transfer of credits, records, and grades
steps: Opened public.law Ed Code 48853.5, read (c)(1)-(2) liaison duties, (f)(1) 'allow the foster child to continue the foster child's education in the school of origin', and (f)(8) 'shall immediately be enrolled in the new school'.

title: Foster Youth Education Liaison
statement: The school district's helper for students in foster care.
source_says: Each local educational agency shall designate a staff person as the educational liaison for foster children.
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: GAL
statement: Guardian ad litem. A person the court appoints to look out for a child's best interests in the case.
source_says: To make recommendations to the court concerning the best interest of the child.
steps: Searched 'rule 5.662 CAPTA guardian ad litem', opened the courts.ca.gov rule page, read the title 'Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act (CAPTA) guardian ad litem' and the general duties.

title: GAL
statement: In California dependency cases, the child's lawyer usually serves as the guardian ad litem.
source_says: An attorney appointed under rule 5.660 will serve as the child's CAPTA guardian ad litem.
steps: Opened the courts.ca.gov rule 5.662 page.

title: GAL
statement: If the child has no lawyer, a CASA volunteer does.
source_says: the court must appoint a CASA volunteer to serve as the child's CAPTA guardian ad litem.
steps: Opened the courts.ca.gov rule 5.662 page.

title: GAL
statement: A person the judge picks to speak up for what is best for a child.
source_says: To make recommendations to the court concerning the best interest of the child.
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: ICWA
statement: Indian Child Welfare Act - Federal law
source_says: Section 1922 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.)
steps: Row has no source listed. Opened public.law WIC 315, which names the federal Act and its U.S. Code cite.

title: ICWA
statement: providing special protections for Native American children and families.
source_says: to protect the best interests of Indian children ... promote the stability and security of Indian tribes and families
steps: Opened law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1902 and read the policy statement, which also refers to 'minimum Federal standards for the removal of' Indian children.

title: ICWA
statement: A law that gives extra protection to Native American children and families.
source_says: to protect the best interests of Indian children
steps: Same page as the definition. Under 25 U.S.C. 1903 the Act covers a child who is a tribal member or eligible and the child of a member, not every child with Native ancestry.

title: ILP
statement: Independent Living Program - services and support for older foster youth (typically 16+) to help them prepare for adulthood.
source_says: Youth are eligible for ILP services from age 16 to the day before their 21st birthday
steps: Searched 'CDSS Independent Living Program eligibility age 16', opened the cdss.ca.gov ILP page. WIC 10609.4, the cited source, does not state the age 16 start; the CDSS page does.

title: ILP
statement: Includes life skills training, education support, and help finding housing and jobs.
source_says: training in daily living skills, budgeting, locating and maintaining housing ... providing job readiness training and placement services
steps: Opened public.law WIC 10609.4; also 'Enabling participants to seek a high school diploma or its equivalent'.

title: ILP
statement: Classes and help for older foster youth to get ready for adult life.
source_says: Youth are eligible for ILP services from age 16 to the day before their 21st birthday
steps: Same CDSS page; it lists Daily living skills, Money management, Employment, Housing (Transitional Housing).

title: Indian Child
statement: Under the Indian Child Welfare Act, a child who is a member of a federally recognized tribe, or who can be a member and is the biological child of a member.
source_says: "Indian child" means any unmarried person who is under age eighteen and is either (a) a member of an Indian tribe
steps: Opened law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1903. Paragraph (4) continues with a person eligible for membership who is the biological child of a member; paragraph (8) ties 'Indian tribe' to federal recognition.

title: Indian Child
statement: Only the tribe decides whether a child is a member or can be one.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 30
source_says: (Note that only tribes can decide if your child is an Indian child.)
steps: Searched for the booklet, opened the courts.ca.gov PDF, read the ICWA part on p. 30.

title: Indian Child
statement: A Native American child covered by a special law. The tribe decides who is a member.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 30
source_says: It applies to your family only if your child is a member of an Indian tribe or is eligible for membership
steps: Same booklet page.

title: Indian Custodian
statement: A Native American person who has legal custody of a Native American child under tribal law or custom or under state law, or who the parent has asked to care for the child for a time.
source_says: "Indian custodian" means any Indian person who has legal custody of an Indian child under tribal law or custom
steps: Opened law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1903(6); the rest of the paragraph covers a person to whom the parent has transferred temporary physical care, custody, and control.

title: Indian Custodian
statement: In a case covered by the Indian Child Welfare Act, an Indian custodian has the right to get notice of hearings
source_says: shall notify the parent or Indian custodian and the Indian child's tribe ... of the pending proceedings and of their right of intervention
steps: Opened law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1912, read subsection (a).

title: Indian Custodian
statement: and to take part in the case.
source_name: 25 U.S.C. 1911(c); Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.530(b)
source_says: the Indian custodian of the child and the Indian child's tribe ... shall have a right to intervene at any point in the proceeding.
steps: Opened law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1911(c). Also opened courts.ca.gov rule 5.530: (b)(2) lists 'All parents, de facto parents, Indian custodians, and guardians of the child' as entitled to be present.

title: Indian Custodian
statement: A Native American adult who is raising a Native American child in place of the parent.
source_says: "Indian custodian" means any Indian person who has legal custody of an Indian child under tribal law or custom
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: Initial Hearing
statement: Another name for the detention hearing, the first hearing in the case.
source_says: In most courts, this is called the detention hearing.
steps: Opened selfhelp.courts.ca.gov guide-parents, read the first-hearing section.

title: Initial Hearing
statement: It must be held by the end of the next court day after the petition is filed.
source_says: If a child has been taken into custody under this article and not released to a parent or guardian ... not later than the expiration of the next judicial day
steps: Opened public.law WIC 315. The next-court-day deadline applies when the child was taken into custody and not released. The Self-Help guide says the same deadline ('by the end of the day after the petition is filed') in a section about a child who was removed. The entry leaves that condition out.
fix: If your child was taken from home and not returned, this hearing must be held by the end of the next court day after the petition is filed.

title: Initial Hearing
statement: The first hearing. Also called the detention hearing.
source_says: In most courts, this is called the detention hearing.
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: Investigation Findings
statement: Substantiated means it more likely than not happened.
source_says: based upon evidence that makes it more likely than not that child abuse or neglect, as defined, occurred.
steps: Opened public.law Penal Code 11165.12 and read all three definitions.

title: Investigation Findings
statement: Inconclusive means there was not enough evidence either way.
source_says: not to be unfounded, but the findings are inconclusive and there is insufficient evidence to determine whether child abuse or neglect, as defined in Section 11165.6, has occurred.
steps: Opened public.law Penal Code 11165.12.

title: Investigation Findings
statement: Unfounded means it was false, an accident, or not abuse or neglect.
source_says: to be false, to be inherently improbable, to involve an accidental injury, or not to constitute child abuse or neglect, as defined in Section 11165.6.
steps: Opened public.law Penal Code 11165.12. The entry leaves out 'inherently improbable', which does not change the meaning.

title: Investigation Findings
statement: What the county decided about a report: it happened, they could not tell, or it did not happen.
source_says: determined by the investigator who conducted the investigation
steps: Same page. The finding is made by the investigator who did the investigation.

title: Jurisdiction
statement: The court's legal power over a child's case. The court takes jurisdiction when the judge finds that what the petition says is true.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 9
source_says: If the judge decides the allegations are true, the court will take authority over your child. This is called jurisdiction in the law
steps: Opened the courts.ca.gov booklet PDF, read p. 9.

title: Jurisdiction
statement: The court's power to make decisions about a child.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 9
source_says: the court will take authority over your child.
steps: Same booklet page.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: The social worker who first looks into a report that a child may not be safe.
source_name: LA County DCFS, Investigations page; Self-Help Guide for parents
source_says: An emergency response social worker will visit your home within five days
steps: Searched for 'emergency response social worker investigates referral', opened dcfs.lacounty.gov/parents/investigations. The cited Self-Help guide describes the investigating social worker but does not use the words 'emergency response'; the CDSS overview page says 'emergency response staff'.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: Some counties call this the investigating worker.
steps: Not stated in the Self-Help guide for parents, the Judicial Council booklet, the CDSS child welfare overview page, or the LA County DCFS investigations page. The shared web search budget for this run ran out before another source could be found.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: They talk with you, your child, and people who know your family, and they look at your home.
source_says: A social worker investigates by talking to you, your child, and people who know you and your family.
steps: Opened selfhelp.courts.ca.gov guide-parents; next sentence is 'They will also look at where you live.'

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: They may talk with your child at school without asking you first, and you are told afterward.
source_says: The social worker can talk to your child at school without you being present. ... they have to tell you that they interviewed your child at school.
steps: Opened guide-parents. The guide's words are 'without you being present', and it adds that no court order is needed 'as long as there is not a police officer present'. The entry does not carry that police detail.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: Then they decide whether to close the report, offer services, or ask the court to open a case.
source_says: Not take any action. ... Offer free services designed to help you learn how to parent your child more safely.
steps: Opened guide-parents and read the list of outcomes; the other two are leaving the child home and filing a petition, or removing the child and filing a petition.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: If the case goes on, you may be assigned a different social worker.
steps: LA County page says 'a DCFS social worker will be assigned to your family' after the investigation but does not say it is a different person. The Self-Help guide and booklet say nothing on this. The shared web search budget for this run ran out before another source could be found.

title: Emergency Response Social Worker
statement: The first social worker you meet. They check whether a child is safe.
source_says: An emergency response social worker will visit your home within five days
steps: Same pages as the definition.

title: Exit Order
statement: A custody order the judge makes when closing a case where the child will live with one parent.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 29
source_says: If your case is dismissed when your child is living with you and not with the child's other parent, the judge will make an exit order.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read pp. 29-30. Also opened public.law WIC 362.4, which lets the juvenile court issue 'an order determining the custody of, or visitation with, the child' when it ends jurisdiction.

title: Exit Order
statement: It says who the child lives with, who makes decisions for the child, and what visits the other parent gets.
source_name: Judicial Council booklet p. 29; form JV-200
source_says: Who the child will live with (called physical custody), and Who can make important decisions for the child, such as medical care, school, and religion (called legal custody).
steps: Opened the booklet. For visits, opened selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/jcc-form/JV-200: 'States the court's decision about where the child lives and what visits can happen after the court ends the dependency case.'

title: Exit Order
statement: It stays in effect after the case closes, and later changes are made in family court.
source_says: shall be a final judgment and shall remain in effect after that jurisdiction is terminated
steps: Opened public.law WIC 302(d) and 362.4 ('shall continue until modified or terminated by a subsequent order of the superior court'). 302(d) adds that a Family Code court may change it only on 'a significant change of circumstances' and the child's best interests. The entry does not say that.

title: Exit Order
statement: form JV-200 (cited as the form for this order)
source_says: Custody Order—Juvenile—Final Judgment
steps: Searched 'JV-200 Custody Order Juvenile Final Judgment', opened the selfhelp.courts.ca.gov form page.

title: Exit Order
statement: The custody order the judge makes when closing the case.
source_says: States the court's decision about where the child lives and what visits can happen after the court ends the dependency case.
steps: Same form page.

title: Extended Foster Care (EFC)
statement: A program that allows youth to stay in foster care until age 21
source_says: Nonminor dependents are eligible to receive support until they reach 21 years of age
steps: Opened public.law WIC 11403 and the cdss.ca.gov Extended Foster Care (AB 12) page ('remain in foster care until age 21').

title: Extended Foster Care (EFC)
statement: if they are working, going to school, or participating in a program to prepare for work or school.
source_says: The nonminor is employed for at least 80 hours per month. ... The nonminor is incapable of doing any of the activities described in paragraphs (1) to (4)
steps: Opened public.law WIC 11403(b): five ways to qualify. The entry lists three, drops the medical condition one, and drops the 80 hours a month. The CDSS page lists 'Be unable to do one of the above because of a medical or mental health condition'.
fix: Youth can stay if they are finishing high school or a program like it, in college or job training, working at least 80 hours a month, in a program that helps them get a job, or not able to do these because of a medical condition.

title: Extended Foster Care (EFC)
statement: Also called AB 12 or Nonminor Dependent status.
source_says: Assembly Bill 12 (AB 12) which became law in 2010 ... are considered non-minor dependents (NMDs)
steps: Searched 'cdss extended foster care AB 12', opened the cdss.ca.gov page.

title: Extended Foster Care (EFC)
statement: Youth must opt in to continue receiving support.
source_says: The youth must sign the Mutual Agreement for Extended Foster Care (form SOC 162) ... after turning age 18 and no later than six months after reaching age 18.
steps: Opened the cdss.ca.gov EFC page. The statute itself does not say 'opt in'; the CDSS page describes the signed agreement.

title: Extended Foster Care (EFC)
statement: You can stay in foster care until 21 if you work, go to school, or are in a program. You have to sign up.
source_says: The nonminor is incapable of doing any of the activities described in paragraphs (1) to (4)
steps: Same as the definition: the simple line also leaves out the medical condition path and the 80 hours a month.
fix: You can stay in foster care until 21 if you are in school or job training, work at least 80 hours a month, are in a job program, or cannot do these because of a medical condition. You sign an agreement to stay.

title: Family Maintenance
statement: When a child stays at home with their parents but the court orders the family to receive services and supervision to keep the child safe.
source_says: the court orders that a parent or guardian shall retain custody of the child ... the supervision of the social worker
steps: Opened public.law WIC 362(c) and WIC 16506 ('in order to maintain the child in his or her own home'). The CDSS overview page also describes Voluntary Family Maintenance without a court order; the entry covers only the court-ordered kind.

title: Family Maintenance
statement: The case is still open but the child is not in foster care.
source_says: where the court has ordered the county welfare department to supervise while the child remains in the child's home
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16506.

title: Family Maintenance
statement: Parents must follow the court's orders.
source_says: the parents or guardians shall be required to participate in child welfare services
steps: Opened public.law WIC 362(c).

title: Family Maintenance
statement: The child stays home, and the family gets help and check-ins from the court.
source_says: where the court has ordered the county welfare department to supervise while the child remains in the child's home
steps: Same pages as the definition.

title: Foster Care
statement: When a child lives with caregivers who are not their parents, usually because it was not safe for them to stay at home.
source_says: "Foster care" means the 24-hour out-of-home care provided to children whose own families are unable or unwilling to care for them
steps: Opened public.law WIC 11400, read subd. (f). The cited source, WIC 16519.5, covers resource family approval, not this definition.

title: Foster Care
statement: Foster parents are approved as resource families to care for children for a time.
source_says: eligible to provide foster care for children in out-of-home placement
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16519.5, read (a), (c)(1), (c)(4)(A), (c)(5).

title: Foster Care
statement: The goal is usually for the child to return home or find a permanent family.
source_says: Reunification means getting your child returned and your family back together.
steps: Opened the booklet (p. 11) and public.law WIC 366.26(b) ('in order to provide stable, permanent homes for these children').

title: Foster Care
statement: When a child lives with other caregivers for a while because home was not safe.
source_says: who are in need of temporary or long-term substitute parenting.
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: Foster Family Agency (FFA)
statement: A nonprofit agency that finds, approves, trains, and supports resource families for the county.

statement: If your child is in a home that works with one, the agency has its own social worker ... in addition to your county social worker.

title: Foster Family Agency (FFA)
statement: [the agency's social worker] visits the home

statement: The county social worker is still in charge of your case.

title: Foster Family Agency (FFA)
statement: A nonprofit agency that finds and supports foster homes for the county.

title: Group Home

title: Group Home
statement: A home where several foster youth live with staff.
source_says: A GH provides 24-hour non-medical care and supervision to children, age 0 through 17
steps: Same page as the definition.

title: Investigation
statement: A social worker or police officer talks with the parent, the child, and people who know the family, and looks at the home.

steps: Opened guide-parents: 'Reports that a child is being abused or neglected are usually made to the police or to social workers.' and 'They will also look at where you live.'

statement: It can end four ways: no action, an offer of free services, a court case with the child staying home, or a court case with the child removed.

steps: Opened guide-parents and read the four listed outcomes, including 'Not take any action.' and leaving the child home while filing a petition.

statement: When a social worker checks whether a child is safe.

statement: The court must be told who the other parent is.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 32; WIC 316.2(a)
source_says: The social worker and the judge will ask you to name your child's other parent
steps: Opened the booklet, p. 32, and WIC 316.2(a) on public.law ('the court shall inquire').

title: Noncustodial Parent
statement: That parent gets notice of hearings
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 32; WIC 290.1
source_says: will send notice of the hearings involving your child to that person
steps: Opened the booklet p. 32 and WIC 290.1 on public.law, which lists the mother and presumed and alleged fathers whose whereabouts are known.

title: Noncustodial Parent
statement: and their own lawyer if they come to court.
source_says: desires counsel but is presently financially unable to afford and cannot for that reason employ counsel
steps: Opened WIC 317. A court lawyer is for a parent who cannot afford one. Under (b) the judge must appoint one when the child is placed out of the home or the county asks for that; otherwise (a) says 'may'. The self-help page for fathers and other parents says an alleged parent may have fewer rights.
fix: If that parent comes to court and cannot pay for a lawyer, they can ask the judge to give them one.

title: Noncustodial Parent
statement: The parent the child was not living with. The child may be able to stay with them.
source_says: with whom the child was not residing at the time that the events or conditions arose
steps: Same page. The self-help guide for parents also lists 'The other parent' as a placement option.

title: Nonminor Dependent
statement: A young adult, 18 to 21, who chooses to stay in foster care under California's extended foster care program.
source_says: until they reach 21 years of age
steps: Searched 'WIC 11403 nonminor dependent 80 hours per month', opened public.law 11403 and 11400. 11400(v)(1): 'has attained 18 years of age while under an order of foster care placement by the juvenile court'. 11400(u)(1): 'A written voluntary agreement of consent for continued placement'.

title: Nonminor Dependent
statement: You qualify if you are finishing high school or an equivalent program, are in college or job training, are in a program that helps you get a job, work at least 80 hours a month, or cannot do these because of a medical condition.
source_says: The nonminor is employed for at least 80 hours per month.
steps: Same page, (b)(1) to (5); all five match. Not in the entry: under WIC 11400(v) the youth must also have turned 18 while under a court order for foster care placement.

title: Nonminor Dependent
statement: A young adult, 18 to 21, who stays in foster care.
source_says: until they reach 21 years of age
steps: Same page.

title: Notice
statement: The official written message telling you the date, time, and place of a hearing and what it is about.
source_says: Service of the notice shall be written or oral
steps: Searched 'WIC 290.1 290.2 notice initial petition hearing', opened public.law 290.1, 290.2 and 291. 291(d) lists 'The nature of the hearing' and 'The date, time, and place of the hearing'. But 290.1(e) lets the social worker give notice of the first hearing out loud, so it is not always written.
fix: The official message telling you the date, time, and place of a hearing and what it is about. It is usually on paper. For the very first hearing, the social worker may tell you out loud.

title: Notice
statement: The court sends notices to the mailing address it has for you
source_says: The court shall advise each parent or guardian that the designated mailing address will be used by the court
steps: Opened WIC 316.1 on public.law and the booklet p. 6 ('so you will get all your mail from the court'). Notices do not always come from the court: 290.1 has the social worker serve the first notice; 290.2 and 291 have the clerk serve later ones; 316.1 says the social services agency uses the same address.

title: Notice
statement: so tell the clerk and your lawyer if you move.
source_says: unless and until the parent or guardian notifies the court ... or the social services agency of a new mailing address in writing
steps: Opened WIC 316.1 and the booklet p. 6 ('tell the judge or court clerk your new address'). The law says the old address keeps being used until the court or the county agency gets the new one in writing. The entry leaves out 'in writing'.
fix: If you move, give the court clerk or your social worker your new address in writing. Tell your lawyer too.

title: Notice
statement: The letter that tells you when and where your hearing is.
source_name: WIC 290.1(e); California Courts Self-Help Guide for parents
source_says: Service of the notice shall be written or oral
steps: Opened WIC 290.1 and the selfhelp.courts.ca.gov guide for parents ('The social worker will tell you when and where the detention hearing is going to take place'). Notice of the first hearing is not always a letter.
fix: The message that tells you when and where your hearing is. It is usually a letter. For the first hearing, the social worker may just tell you.

title: Ombudsperson
statement: The California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson helps foster youth who have problems or complaints.
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, home page
source_says: a neutral and independent office that helps solve problems and complaints
steps: Searched 'Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson fosteryouthhelp.ca.gov', opened the home page, Contact Us, File a Complaint and Our Services pages. Contact Us gives the name 'The California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson'.

title: Ombudsperson
statement: Foster youth can call or email the Ombudsperson confidentially to report issues like mistreatment, rights violations, or problems with their placement.
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, home page and File a Complaint page
source_says: We have a confidentiality policy to protect the identity of people who call to make a complaint.
steps: Opened the home page and File a Complaint page ('We have jurisdiction over foster youth rights, care, placement, and services'; email fosteryouthhelp@dss.ca.gov). The home page adds that the law allows some sharing of information during an investigation and that the office may report urgent safety concerns to child protection or licensing, after talking with the caller.
fix: Foster youth can call or email the Ombudsperson about things like mistreatment, rights not being respected, or problems with their placement. The office keeps your name private. If someone is in danger, it may have to tell a child protection or licensing agency, and it will talk with you about that.

title: Ombudsperson
statement: It's free and confidential.
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, home page
source_says: contact our toll free hotline at 877-846-1602
steps: Same home page. The call is toll free. The privacy promise has limits: the office protects the caller's identity but may share some information in an investigation and may report urgent safety concerns.
fix: The call is free. The office keeps your name private, but it may have to report it if someone is in danger.

title: Ombudsperson
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, Contact Us
steps: Opened the Contact Us page. Hours shown: 'Open Monday - Friday from 8AM - 5PM'.

title: Ombudsperson
statement: A state office foster youth can call for free when something is wrong.
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, home page
source_says: contact our toll free hotline at 877-846-1602
steps: Same home page: 'Our office was created to serve foster youth'.

title: Ombudsperson
statement: What you say is kept private.
source_name: California Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, home page
source_says: We have a confidentiality policy to protect the identity of people who call to make a complaint.
steps: Same home page. The policy protects who you are. The page says some information can be shared in an investigation and urgent safety concerns may be reported.
fix: They keep your name private. If someone is in danger, they may have to tell people who can help.

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: The lawyer who represents you, the parent, in dependency court. If you cannot afford a lawyer, the court appoints one for you.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 3; WIC 317(a)-(b)
source_says: Have a lawyer; the judge will give you one if you cannot afford to hire your own.
steps: Opened the booklet p. 3 and p. 8, the self-help guide for parents ('If you cannot afford a lawyer, the judge will assign one to you'), and WIC 317. Under 317(b) the judge must appoint when the child is placed out of the home or the county asks for that; under 317(a) the judge 'may' in other cases.

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: The court may ask later whether you can pay back some of the cost, based on what you can afford.
source_says: the court determines that the person has the ability to pay all or part of the costs
steps: Searched 'WIC 903.1 cost of legal services dependency', opened public.law 903.1 ('shall be liable for the cost to the county or the court') and 903.45(b). 903.1(b): nobody owes this if the petition 'is dismissed at or before the jurisdictional hearing'. Santa Clara court page: 'You may be charged for the lawyer fees if the Court determines that you have the ability to pay.'

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: Your lawyer explains what is happening in court, goes over the social worker's report with you, speaks for you at hearings, and can file papers asking the judge to change an order or return your child.
source_says: Counsel shall represent the parent, guardian, child, or nonminor dependent at the detention hearing and at all subsequent proceedings before the juvenile court.
steps: Opened WIC 317(d) and the booklet: p. 23 'You should talk with your attorney before each hearing date to find out what the report means'; p. 33 'You will need a lawyer's help to file a 388.'

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: Each parent usually has their own lawyer.
source_name: San Bernardino Superior Court, Dependency Hearings
source_says: Attorneys are appointed by the court for each child and parent/guardian for each case.
steps: The three cited sources (WIC 317, the booklet, WIC 903.1) do not say this. Searched for court pages on parents' lawyers and opened the San Bernardino court page, which says the court 'appoints an attorney to represent each parent/guardian and child'. This is one county's page.

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: Meet with your lawyer before every hearing and keep asking questions until you understand.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, pp. 22-23
source_says: You should talk with your attorney before each hearing date to find out what the report means.
steps: Opened the booklet. p. 22: 'Ask questions if there's anything you don't understand!'

title: Parent's Attorney
statement: The parent's own lawyer. You get one even if you cannot pay.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 3
source_says: Have a lawyer; the judge will give you one if you cannot afford to hire your own.
steps: Same booklet page. The simple line leaves out that the court may later ask the parent to pay some of the cost back (WIC 903.1, 903.45).

title: Parentage
statement: The court's word for who a child's legal parents are.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, If you want to be included in your child's dependency case
source_says: Parentage is a word used in dependency court to refer to a child's parents.
steps: Searched for the self-help guide on parents' right to be included, opened the selfhelp.courts.ca.gov page.

title: Parentage
statement: A person can be a legal parent without a blood tie.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, If you want to be included in your child's dependency case
source_says: you may qualify as a parent even if you are not biologically related to the child
steps: Same page.

title: Parentage
statement: At the first hearing the judge asks about every possible parent.
source_says: At the detention hearing, or as soon thereafter as practicable ... the identity and address of all presumed or alleged fathers
steps: Searched 'WIC 316.2 court shall inquire presumed or alleged fathers', opened public.law. The statute says fathers; the self-help guide says the court asks about 'anyone who may qualify as a father or other parent to the child'.

title: Parentage
statement: Who the law says a child's parents are.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, If you want to be included in your child's dependency case
source_says: Parentage is a word used in dependency court to refer to a child's parents.
steps: Same page.

title: Party
statement: A person or agency with the legal right to take part in the case, get notice, and be heard.
source_name: Santa Clara Superior Court, Participants in Dependency Cases
source_says: A party is someone who has the right to: Go to court, Be heard, and, Have a lawyer at the hearing
steps: Neither cited source defines 'party', so searched court pages and opened the Santa Clara court page. Its list is go to court, be heard, have a lawyer. Notice to parents and children is set by WIC 290.1 and 291, which were opened for the Notice entry.

title: Party
statement: The child, the parents, and the county agency are parties.
source_name: WIC 317.5(b); Santa Clara Superior Court page; rule 5.502(29)
source_says: Each minor who is the subject of a dependency proceeding is a party to that proceeding.
steps: Opened WIC 317.5 on public.law (child). Santa Clara page: 'In a Dependency case, a party can be' the mother, the father, the child, the social worker, a legal guardian, or a de facto parent. Rule 5.502(29): the petitioner 'means the county welfare department'.

title: Party
statement: In a case under the Indian Child Welfare Act, the child's tribe can be a party too.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(e); Judicial Council booklet p. 30
source_says: The tribe of an Indian child is entitled to intervene as a party
steps: Searched for the tribe's right to intervene, opened rule 5.534 on courts.ca.gov. Booklet p. 30: 'When the tribe intervenes, you may hear the legal term that the tribe is a party to the case.'

title: Party
statement: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.530
source_says: Rule 5.530. Persons present
steps: Opened rule 5.530. It lists who may be in the courtroom. It does not define 'party' or say who the parties are. The points in the entry are in WIC 317.5(b) and rule 5.534(e). The booklet uses 'party' only for the tribe (p. 30).
fix: Source: WIC 317.5(b); Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534; Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You.

title: Party
statement: Someone who has the right to take part in the court case.
source_name: Santa Clara Superior Court, Participants in Dependency Cases
source_says: A party is someone who has the right to: Go to court, Be heard, and, Have a lawyer at the hearing
steps: Same page.

title: Permanency
statement: A stable, long-term living situation for a child.
source_says: in order to provide stable, permanent homes for these children
steps: Opened WIC 366.26 on public.law, read the opening of (b).

title: Permanency
statement: The goal is for every child to have a permanent family - either by returning home to their parents, being adopted, living with a legal guardian, or (for older teens) having a stable long-term placement with connections to caring adults.
source_says: the child will be returned to the parent ... placed for adoption ... or referred for legal guardianship ... a child who has attained 16 years of age
steps: Searched '42 U.S.C. 675(5)(C) permanency plan', opened law.cornell.edu and WIC 366.26. 'Older teens' means 16 or older in both laws. The entry leaves out two listed choices: placement with 'a fit and willing relative' (366.26(b)(6)) and tribal customary adoption (366.26(b)(2)).

title: Permanency
statement: A home that lasts.
source_says: in order to provide stable, permanent homes for these children
steps: Same page.

title: Permanency Hearing
statement: A hearing held about 12 months after your child entered foster care, and again by 18 months.
source_says: The permanency hearing shall be held no later than 12 months after the date the child entered foster care
steps: Opened WIC 366.21 and 366.22 on public.law. The 18-month hearing is held only if the judge continues the case at 12 months (366.21(g)(1): 'Continue the case for up to 6 months for a permanency review hearing'). Its clock runs from removal: 366.22(a)(1) 'within 18 months after the date the child was originally removed'.
fix: A hearing held no later than 12 months after your child entered foster care. If the judge gives you more time, there is one more hearing within 18 months of the day your child was removed.

title: Permanency Hearing
statement: The judge must return your child to you unless the county shows that would not be safe.
source_says: would create a substantial risk of detriment to the safety, protection, or physical or emotional well-being of the child
steps: Same pages. Both sections say the court 'shall order the return of the child' unless it finds that risk by a preponderance of the evidence, and 'The social worker shall have the burden of establishing that detriment.'

title: Permanency Hearing
statement: If your child is not returned, the judge may give you more time or set a hearing to choose a permanent plan.
source_says: Continue the case for up to 6 months for a permanency review hearing ... Order that a hearing be held within 120 days, pursuant to Section 366.26
steps: Same page, (g). More time needs a finding that return is likely in that time or that reasonable services were not provided. At 18 months, 366.22(a)(3) says the court 'shall order' the 366.26 hearing unless the narrow conditions in (b) are met.

title: Permanency Hearing
statement: The hearing at 12 months, and again by 18 months, where the judge decides if your child can come home.
source_says: shall occur within 18 months after the date the child was originally removed
steps: Same pages. There is an 18-month hearing only when the judge continued the case at 12 months.
fix: The hearing at 12 months where the judge decides if your child can come home. If the judge gives more time, there is one more by 18 months.

title: Permanency Planning Hearing
statement: Also called the .26 hearing or 366.26 hearing.
source_name: Judicial Council dependency flow chart; Judicial Council booklet p. 15
source_says: PERMANENCY PLANNING/ W&I 366.26 HEARINGS
steps: Searched 'permanency planning hearing 366.26 courts.ca.gov', opened the courts.ca.gov flow chart. Booklet p. 15: 'it looks like .26 or 366.26'. Rule 5.725 is titled 'Selection of permanent plan' and San Bernardino's court page calls it 'Selection & Implementation', so families may hear those names too.

title: Permanency Planning Hearing
statement: This is the hearing to decide on a permanent plan for the child when reunification has failed.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 15; WIC 366.21(g)(4)
source_says: If the judge terminates your reunification services and CPS thinks that your child should be adopted or in a legal guardianship, you will get a paper from the court
steps: Opened the booklet p. 15 and WIC 366.21(g)(4) ('Order that a hearing be held within 120 days, pursuant to Section 366.26').

title: Permanency Planning Hearing
statement: The court considers termination of parental rights to free the child for adoption, or other permanent plans like legal guardianship.
source_says: Terminate the rights of the parent or parents and order that the child be placed for adoption ... Appoint a nonrelative legal guardian for the child
steps: Opened WIC 366.26 on public.law, read the list in (b). Rule 5.725: 'The purpose of termination of parental rights is to free the child for adoption.'

title: Permanency Planning Hearing
statement: The hearing to pick a long-term home when the child is not going back to their parents. Also called the .26 hearing.
source_name: Judicial Council, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 15
source_says: This is the plan naming whom your child will live with for the long term.
steps: Same booklet page: 'What is a .26 (two-six) hearing?'

title: Petitioner
statement: The one who files the petition that starts the case.
source_says: is commenced by the filing with the court, by the social worker, of a petition
steps: Searched 'WIC 325 commenced by the filing with the court by the social worker of a petition', opened the FindLaw code page (public.law was not in the results).

title: Petitioner
statement: In dependency court that is the county social services agency.
source_says: "Petitioner," in section 300 proceedings, means the county welfare department
steps: Opened rule 5.502 on courts.ca.gov, read the definition. The cited rule 5.530(d) only says the county counsel or district attorney 'must appear and represent the petitioner'; the definition is in rule 5.502.

title: Petitioner
statement: In court papers, "the petitioner" means the county.
source_says: "Petitioner," in section 300 proceedings, means the county welfare department
steps: Same rule page.

title: Petitioner
statement: The one who started the court case. In these cases it is the county.
source_says: "Petitioner," in section 300 proceedings, means the county welfare department
steps: Same sources.
